quotes.quote: Caridina woltereckae is endemic to Lake Towuti, the largest of the five connected lakes of the Malili lake system, Sulawesi, Indonesia.

sections.html:
• Common names: Harlequin Shrimp, Sulawesi shrimp
  • Tank size (minimum – optimal): 20 – 40 litres
  • Breeding: medium-difficult
  • KH: 4 – 5
  • TDS: 146 – 175 µS/cm or 75 – 90 ppm
  • Nitrate: less than 10 ppm
  • Diet: algae eater/omnivore
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Colour: reddish (or dark-brown) bands around the carapace

Caridina woltereckae is a relatively rare dwarf shrimp that needs very specific care. It is not for beginners and is more difficult to keep than most other shrimp species.

The species is currently under threat due to overharvesting for the aquarium trade, pollution and invasive fish species.

The colour morph closely resembles Caridina spongicola, so the two can easily be misidentified, and some shops may sell this species under other names. C. woltereckae is found in all parts of Lake Towuti, averages 1.8 cm, is vividly or contrastingly coloured with distinctive sidelines, lives on rocks and has a longer rostrum reaching beyond the end of the scaphocerite. C. spongicola is found in the outlet bay of Lake Towuti, averages 1.5 cm, has inconsistent colour with fuzzy, almost absent sidelines, occurs on sponges and has a shorter rostrum reaching to or slightly beyond the third segment of the antennular peduncle.

It is important not to confuse them: C. spongicola is the only freshwater shrimp that lives in association with a yet undescribed freshwater sponge of the suborder Spongillina, which it needs to survive, so keeping it in aquariums can be extremely difficult.
Caridina woltereckae is endemic to Lake Towuti, the largest of the five connected lakes of the Malili lake system, Sulawesi, Indonesia.

These shrimp are only found on hard substrate, mainly between small rocks in shallow water and on large rocks in deeper water (below 3 m). According to collectors, when disturbed they try to escape sideways or downwards rather than in other directions, but mostly stay attached to rocks.

The minimum recommended tank is 20 litres; ideally 40 litres suits them much better. Stable water parameters are hard to achieve in small tanks, even for experienced aquarists. Given their small size, a 40-litre tank can easily hold at least 40 – 50 shrimp.

Cycle the tank before adding shrimp, then wait at least a few more weeks so the tank develops a stable ecosystem with biofilm and algae as a natural food source.

Do not keep them in planted tanks. They do not eat healthy plants, but in planted tanks pH often fluctuates slightly: when the lights are off, plants stop taking in CO2 and producing oxygen, so more carbonic acid forms and pH drops. These shrimp are very delicate and even small fluctuations add risk.

Before adding them, acclimate them carefully and very slowly over a few hours. Like all crustaceans, they do not tolerate copper-based medications.

If you buy captive-bred shrimp (several generations), find out the water parameters they were bred in. If this is unknown, presume the breeder kept them close to natural values, i.e. replicate the water of Lake Towuti.

  • Temperature: 28.7 – 29.2 °C. A heater is needed; they prefer warm water and can get shocked if the temperature drops below 25 °C.
  • Hardness: GH 6 – 7, KH 4 – 5. They do not like hard water.
  • pH: 8.4 – 8.5
  • TDS: 146 – 175 µS/cm or 75 – 90 ppm
  • Oxygen: 7.15 mg/l. An extra air pump may be needed; low oxygen can be a real problem.

Keeping them in tap water is almost impossible. RO/DI water remineralised with a special supplement is highly recommended. Sulawesi Mineral 8.5 was developed from analysis of Lake Towuti water.

Lighting: they are nocturnal and do not really depend on light.

Substrate: they prefer a rocky substrate with some sand.

Filter: no special requirements; any filter suited to the tank size will do. Sponge or matten filters are recommended for small tanks: they are cheap, easy to maintain and provide plenty of surface to graze on.

Decorations provide more surface for algae and biofilm, plus hiding places that reduce stress, which is also crucial for moulting. There should be plenty of dark areas made of rocks, PVC pipe, plastic tunnels, etc. Be careful with large pieces of driftwood: tannins may cause pH fluctuations.

They are scavengers and omnivores and will eat almost any food they find. In a well-established tank they usually find enough food (algae, debris, biofilm, etc.) themselves. To keep them healthy or enhance colour, supplement with vegetables and commercial foods such as Dennerle Shrimp King, Hikari Shrimp Cuisine and Glassgarden Shrimp Dinner Food Pads. Dry leaves and blanched vegetables (carrot, sprouts, spinach, cucumber, zucchini, etc.) provide the micronutrients needed for moulting.

Feeding in the evening is better, as they come out and feed better when the lights are low or off.

Like all crustaceans, they have an exoskeleton hardened by calcium salts, so enough calcium is essential, supplied by regularly feeding specialised invertebrate foods or calcium-rich vegetables.

In a mature tank (with algae and biofilm) they can be fed once every 2 – 3 days. It is better to underfeed than overfeed: overfeeding is one of the biggest causes of death in dwarf shrimp, especially sensitive species like this one. Uneaten food and organic waste decompose quickly and cause infections, parasites, and ammonia and nitrate spikes.

They are completely peaceful and very shy. They are nocturnal: activity starts at sunset and gradually stops before sunrise. They are social and prefer the company of their own species; larger colonies often have more active members that venture out more often, so they should ideally be kept in large groups.
Females generally reach 1.8 cm; males usually do not grow larger than 1.5 cm.

Breeding in captivity is not easy but possible; they usually do not breed until the environment is optimal. Mating is very brief (a few seconds) and potentially dangerous for females, which must moult before spawning, making them vulnerable.

Ovigerous females carry 20 – 30 eggs of around 1 mm, which take 3 – 4 weeks to hatch. There is no larval stage: what emerges is a tiny copy of the adult.

Balance feeding with powdered food. Baby shrimp do not move around as much as adults, so they may starve if they do not find enough food.

Lifespan: with proper setup and optimum conditions they can live up to 1.5 years in captivity.

Tankmates: the ideal is a species-only tank, possibly with hardy snails such as Rabbit snails (Tylomelania), which have similar requirements. They should not be kept even with other popular Sulawesi shrimp such as Cardinal shrimp (Caridina dennerli), as these prefer a different pH.

Taxonomy: in 2009 the taxonomy of Sulawesi freshwater shrimp was partially revised and Caridina woltereckae and Caridina mahalona were described. The species is named after the German naturalist Eva Roth-Woltereck (1911 – 2003), who described several Sulawesi atyid shrimp in the 1930s.
